introFa: کتاب «The Narrow Corridor: States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty» نوشته Daron Acemoglu & James A. Robinson یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.

واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Critical Dialogue Critical Dialogue The Narrow Corridor: States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty. By Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson. New York: Penguin Press, 2019. 576p. $32.00 cloth. doi:10.1017/S1537592720001838 — Sheri Berman , Barnard College, Columbia University sberman@barnard.edu Throughout their careers Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson have tackled big questions. What are the origins of dictatorship and democracy? Why do nations fail? Why are some countries prosperous while others remain mired in poverty? With their latest book, The Narrow Corridor: States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty, Acemoglu and Robinson continue along their ambitious path, seeking to understand nothing less than “how and why human societies have achieved or failed to achieve” liberty (p. xi). Liberty, for Acemoglu and Robinson, is “the absence of dominance”: individuals must be “free to choose their actions,” as well as have “the ability to exercise that freedom.” (Although they do not put it this way, Acemoglu and Robinson favor a “positive” rather than a “negative” concep- tion of liberty.) This type of liberty is rare in human history, emerging only in very particular contexts or, as they put it, when countries ﬁnd themselves within a narrow corridor. In contrast to libertarians and other advocates of a minimal state, Acemoglu and Robinson argue that a neces- sary condition for liberty is a strong state capable of main- taining order and providing a wide range of public goods. But although a strong state is necessary for liberty, it is not suﬃcient. Indeed, Acemoglu and Robinson argue that a strong state can be antithetical to liberty, because a state strong enough to maintain order and provide a wide range of public goods is also strong enough to dominate society. So, if neither an Absent nor a Despotic Leviathan will do, what will? Acemoglu and Robinson argue what is required is a Shackled Leviathan: a “state [with] the capacity to enforce laws, control violence, resolve conﬂicts and provide public services” but one that is “tamed and controlled by an assertive, well-organized society” (p. 24). Liberty, in short, requires a strong state balanced by a strong society. This is a wise and important point and parallels arguments by other scholars of state development and state-society relations like Michael Mann, Peter Evans, Joel Migdal, and Andreas Wimmer. There are, however, some vagaries associated with Acemoglu and Robinson’s description of the context within which liberty ﬂourishes. First, Acemoglu and Robinson deﬁne a strong society as one able to “contend, constrain, and check” the state (p. 146). But this deﬁnition is tautological: it assesses the independent variable (society’s strength) by the dependent variable (its ability to shackle the state). With- out an independent measure of society’s strength, it is hard to evaluate statements like the following—“if the state and elites become too powerful, we end up with the Despotic Leviathan. If they fall behind, we get the Absent Levia- than” (p. 40)—because we have no way of assessing whether states or societies are becoming “stronger” or “weaker” separate from the outcome being described: an “out of balance” relationship between them. Two meas- ures of society’s strength that would ﬁt Acemoglu and Robinson’s analysis are the density and nature (reinforcing or cross-cutting) of its civil society organizations, because these critically shape whether citizens can cooperate, over- come collective action problems, engage in political action, and so on. This raises a second important point that Acemoglu and Robinson discuss but perhaps do not fully grapple with. They stress the “strength” or “weakness” (however meas- ured) of states and societies as crucial, but the nature of states and societies is equally important. Divided and polarized societies, for example, may be “strong” in the sense of being highly mobilized, organized, and participa- tory, but such societies are less capable of (or interested in?) checking despotic states than uniﬁed ones. Similarly, states can be strong in the sense of being able to maintain order, provide public goods, and so on, but their power can be exercised or institutionalized in dramatically diﬀerent ways. The Prussian and late nineteenth/early twentieth- century German states, for example, were “strong” but were constructed in a way that cemented the power of antiliberal, antidemocratic elites, making it harder for a society capable of shackling them to develop and thus for liberty to ﬂourish. A third issue concerns democracy. Interestingly, dem- ocracy is not directly emphasized in Acemoglu and Robin- son’s description of what makes a society able to shackle the state. But is not democracy a necessary, but surely not suﬃcient condition, for a society to be able to mobilize, organize, protest, and so on? Relatedly, without © The Author(s), 2020. institutionalized mechanisms to check executives, main- tain the rule of law, ensure that citizens are able to get rid of leaders who are unresponsive to them, and so on, how can the state be deterred from dominating society? The Narrow Corridor’s relative lack of emphasis on democracy may be related to a distinction between the conditions necessary for the emergence and maintenance of liberty, with democ- racy being more important for the latter than the former. This brings me to another question I had about The Narrow Corridor. Acemoglu and Robinson’s ﬁrst contri- bution is to make the case that a balance between a strong state and society creates the narrow corridor within which liberty ﬂourishes. But they say that they are not just describing the context within which liberty ﬂourishes but also providing a theory. Typically, theories provide answers to “why” questions; in this case, why some countries, at some times, fall into and out of the narrow corridor. The Narrow Corridor provides innumerable fas- cinating discussions of various societies’ political paths from ancient times to the present, but I was unable to pull out of these discussions a clear, systematic argument about which variables determine why or when the “right” state–society balance appears. Acemoglu and Robinson reject many of the most prominent existing theories about the development of states, societies, and the relationship between them. They treat war as a dependent rather than an independent variable, aﬀected by the balance between state and society rather than aﬀecting that balance. They argue, for example, that warfare in early modern Europe pushed Prussia, but not Switzerland, toward despotism, because Swiss society was able to counterbalance an increasingly powerful state. They view technological change similarly. Examining the contemporary period, for example, Ace- moglu and Robinson argue that whether new technologies will increase the despotic powers of the state depends on the strength of society: in Denmark, where society is strong, the state’s despotic powers are less like to increase as a result of technological change than in China, where society is weak. Acemoglu and Robinson also reject mod- ernization theory. They do not believe, for example, that economic development alone will change Chinese society enough to shift the country oﬀits long-standing despotic path. In their own discussions of countries’ political paths, Acemoglu and Robinson sometimes stress structural fac- tors and historical legacies as the key variables pushing countries down diﬀerent political paths. For example, they argue that the answer to the question of why Europe experienced an “unprecedented rise of liberty…lies in a unique series of historical events 1,500 years ago that created a fortuitous balance between the powers of central authority and those of common men.… It is this balance that put Europe into the corridor” (p. 153). Particularly important was the takeover of Europe at the end of the ﬁfth century by “democratically organized tribal societies centered on assemblies and norms of consensual decision making” and “state institutions” inherited from the Roman Empire and the Christian Church (pp. 153, 199). There is no explanation, however, for why the advantageous legacies of these historical events persisted over time, whereas other historical legacies less conducive to the rise of liberty, such as religious intolerance, obscur- antism, and a caste-like system of estates, did not. Yet, despite the attention paid to structural factors and historical legacies, The Narrow Corridor also clearly con- fronts the limits to such variables or explanations. Some countries, for example, despite auspicious background conditions, fall out of the narrow corridor. Europe is in this camp, because the continent fell in and out of the narrow corridor many times between 500 AD and the modern era, even though its ancient legacies prepared the scene for the rise of the Shackled Leviathan, thus making clear that “history is not destiny” (p. 302). Other coun- tries, meanwhile, lacking auspicious background condi- tions, nevertheless sometimes manage to shift into the narrow corridor, something Acemoglu and Robinson often attribute to the actions of political leaders who have an “edge” (by which I think they mean extraordinary political skills or charisma), a “will to power,” and an ability to form coalitions to support their political projects. Given the historical and global range of the cases examined in The Narrow Corridor, it is not surprising that history turns out to be “messy.” Indeed, it is hard to imagine that a single or perhaps even one type of variable could explain something as complex as the emergence or maintenance of liberty. But given political science’s cur- rent mania for “causal identiﬁcation,” I think it is worth being clear about what we can and should expect from diﬀerent types of analyses. Perhaps theory building—in the sense of oﬀering an independent variable that can be clearly connected to a particular dependent variable—is not possible when tack- ling big questions like the emergence or maintenance of liberty. Perhaps that type of simple, straightforward ana- lysis is only suitable for very limited situations—one where the analyst can manipulate variables, be satisﬁed with somewhat thin and superﬁcial understandings of causality, or is willing to identify only the last link in complex causal chains, as experiments do, for example. But unless we, as a ﬁeld, are willing to abandon the big questions, a diﬀerent understanding of our goals is necessary. In my 2019 book, Democracy and Dictatorship in Europe, for example, I do not identify a particular inde- pendent variable or set of variables or claim to have a theory that explains political development across time and space. What the book oﬀers instead is an analysis of European political history from the ancien régime to the present day that identiﬁes patterns of or generalizations about how political development occurred. I wonder if that 904 Perspectives on Politics Critical Dialogue https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592720001863

is, in fact, what Acemoglu and Robinson aimed to provide in The Narrow Corridor, rather than a “theory” in the more traditional sense. If, however, Acemoglu and Robinson do indeed want to oﬀer a theory of why some countries end up within the narrow corridor, and not a description of that corridor—an endeavor, I want to stress, that I believe is important, diﬃcult, and undervalued by our discipline—or some generalizations about how that corridor has historically emerged or been maintained, then some questions naturally present themselves. What are the most important variables pushing countries into or out of the narrow corridor? Do wise, determined, politically savvy leaders always have the possibility of shifting their country’s political path or are particular preconditions for such dramatic shifts necessary? If so, what are they? Are the conditions favoring the emergence of liberty the same as conditions enabling its maintenance? If not, how do they diﬀer? Response to Sheri Berman’s Review of The Narrow Corridor: States, Societies, and the Fate of Liberty doi:10.1017/S1537592720001863 — Daron Acemoglu, James A. Robinson Sheri Berman raises some important questions about our book The Narrow Corridor. She asks how the “strength of society” should be measured. She proceeds to suggest that measuring the density and nature of its civil society organizations is one promising idea. We agree and gave several instances of what we mean by the strength of civil society in the book; for example, in our discussion of Charles Tilly’s (1995) book Popular Contention in Great Britain, where he shows how society formed diﬀerent types of associations and organizations in response to the threats created by the eighteenth-century British state. This measure coincides with Berman’s intuition. But we did not want to equate the strength of society with Western-type notions of civil society. Society in Yemen is strong, but it does not look like the Western notion. Rather, it is organized around lineages and extended kin groups, or “tribes.” Similarly, as we also discussed in the book, in Africa, society was organized by secret societies, age sets, and title associations: even if these do not look like civil society, they provide a rich set of empirical patterns relevant for understanding the strength of society. Berman also asks whether one should probe more the diﬀerent natures of society. For example, society can, in addition to being strong, be “divided and polarized” in ways that make it very diﬃcult for it to check the power of the state. That is exactly our theory in fact, especially as we explain in detail in the context of India in chapter 8. Indian society was “strong” in an organizational sense in many ways, but as we show there, it was divided against itself along the lines of caste. As a result, it could not do an eﬀective job of balancing the state. This is where our argument about the “Red Queen eﬀect” comes in. When we talk about the strength of society, we are factoring in how the nature of society alters endogenously in the course of its struggle with the state, especially in the corridor. Do we underemphasize democracy? We do not think so. But we do not equate society’s organization and strength with democracy. That might appear natural from a European perspective, but it is not justiﬁed by the history of many non-European places, where societies could be organized and rulers kept in check, even if they did not look like a typical democracy. Even in Europe, as our argument in chapter 6 illustrates, society’s strength long predates the types of institutions we typically associate with democracy. Finally, Berman asks, Do we have a theory? It is useful to ask ﬁrst what Berman means by a “theory.” Some social scientists equate a theory with a holistic explanation for the phenomenon at hand. Some go further and want the main drivers in the theory to be “exogenous” factors, such as geography, endowments, or historically predetermined events. We do not think this is the right way to think about a theory. Explaining a phenomenon such as dem- ocracy with agricultural conditions that favor wheat is no more or no less a theory than an approach that emphasizes the nature of political coalitions or the role of leaders but at the same time points out when diﬀerent types of coalitions are more likely (but deﬁnitely not certain) to emerge. More fundamentally, a theory, as we understand it, is all about clarifying mechanisms, so that we can think about the phenomenon of interest in a more nuanced way and answer questions about why something has or has not happened. This again highlights the importance of “com- parative statics”: What are the characteristics that make this phenomenon more or less likely to happen? According to these criteria, our entire book is centered on a theory and is about developing this theory. First, we propose a new mechanism. We argue that the roots of liberty and institutions, such as democratic ones, that protect liberty and keep elites in check lie in the balance of power between state and society. Second, we explain, at least in broad terms, how path dependence and speciﬁc societal choices in the relevant historical circumstances shape the trajectories of nations. Think, for example, of our account of how the conjunction of the collapse of the Western Roman Empire and the bottom-up politics of the Frankish tribes that ﬁlled the ensuing void created new opportunities that were exploited by leaders such as Clovis and Charlemagne and how this created a path-dependent process of evolution of states and societies in the corridor. Finally, as we recount in chapter 9, our approach delivers some powerful and unique comparative statics; for instance, emphasizing how the same set of circumstances will lead to divergent outcomes in terms of despotism, September 2020 | Vol. 18/No. 3 905 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592720001863

statelessness, or liberty depending on the prevailing bal- ance of power. Democracy and Dictatorship in Europe: From the Ancien Régime to the Present Day. By Sheri Berman. New York: Oxford University Press, 2019. 560p. $34.95 cloth. doi:10.1017/S1537592720002224 — Daron Acemoglu, James A. Robinson , MIT, University of Chicago daron@mit.edu, jamesrobinson@uchicago.edu Liberal democracy seems under threat from all sides. The international institutions supporting the liberal demo- cratic project, like the European Union, teeter on the brink, while the president of the United States argues at the United Nations that “the future does not belong to globalists; the future belongs to patriots.” One wonders, surrounded by such enemies, how liberal democracy ever managed to be created in the ﬁrst place. The answer, revealed in this thought-provoking new book by Sheri Berman, is that the creation was very recent, after World War II, and even then, it was touch and go. Why so recently? The notion of democracy in Europe is old, dating at least to classical Greece, and notions of liberalism were widespread by the seventeenth century and already fused, at least in the work of John Locke, with notions of democratic representation and accountability. But there were always some ﬂies in the ointment. Aristotle, who keenly observed Athenian democracy with all of its active citizen participation, did not approve of it. Democracy, as far as he was concerned, was a “deviant” form of constitution, pregnant with danger. Locke understood well that achieving liberty, or what he described as a situation where men were in “a state of perfect freedom to order their actions … as they think ﬁt … without asking leave, or depending on the Will of any other Man,” required a particular institutionalization. But he did not articulate a positive theory of how democracy would arise and whether it would be stable in the face of challenges. Modern political scientists have usually signed up to notions of “modernization” whereby economic development and rising educational attainment naturally bring out liberal democracy. Unfortunately, the facts do not support this claim (see Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, James A. Robinson, and Pierre Yared, “From Education to Democracy?” American Economic Review 95 [2], 2005; “Income and Democracy,” American Eco- nomic Review 98 [3], 2008). So where does liberal dem- ocracy come from? Berman’s book takes us into the deep historical roots of liberal democracy in Western Europe and its somewhat unlikely emergence. The main reason for this is that liberal democracy “requires transforming not merely the political procedures and institutions of dictatorship, but societies and economies as well” (p. 386). The types of institutions Locke sketched out in his Second Treatise are not stable on their own and collapse if they do not sit on top of the right type of society. Although this might sound like modern- ization theory redux, it is not. Berman does emphasize that “it often takes powerful structural forces like economic development or violent events like war or revolution to uproot” the “social and economic legacies of the old order” (p. 391). Her focus, however, is much more on the violence than economic development. In addition, Ber- man argues that there are two types of interrelated insti- tutional and social prerequisites; a strong central state and the creation of a national identity. Indeed, a key ﬁnding of the book is that “the sequencing of state-, nation-, and democracy-building mattered” (p. 391) and “liberal dem- ocracy … has consolidated only in countries possessing relatively strong states and national unity” (p. 392). But she also points out that the types of states that formed and how they went about trying to create national unity mattered, observing, “As opposed to dictatorships, demo- cratic and particularly liberal-democratic regimes have at least the potential to promote national unity and cohesion as well as potentially a greater ability to integrate diverse groups into a national whole” (p. 396). Now one begins to see why, in Berman’s view, liberal democracy could only ﬁnally emerge in the wake of World War II. It was only during this time that the last vestiges of nonliberal interests and institutions were swept away. Yet even then liberal democracy’s existence was precarious. It depended not just on domestic factors but also on coord- ination between countries, and it required intensive inter- vention in the economy so that mass unemployment or inequality did not emerge. These changes created a posi- tive feedback loop so that “by showing how broadly responsive liberal democracy could be, the postwar order helped to undercut the appeal of anti-democratic extrem- ists on the left and right who claimed only non-liberal democratic regimes could truly represent ‘the people’” (p. 400). Berman’s book is a salutary reminder of how recently both the Left and the Right were following in Aristotle’s footsteps in rejecting democracy as a deviant political form. Berman then concludes that liberal dem- ocracy is now threatened because many of its critical preconditions have come unstuck. There is much to like about the book—and much to learn from it. Berman is surely right that one cannot understand the emergence of liberal democracy without grasping the historical dynamics. It is equally true that even in the places with the best initial conditions, such as Britain, the process was highly volatile and violent. This is, in fact, what we tried to capture with the notion of the “Red Queen eﬀect” in The Narrow Corridor: democratic institutions and the protection of liberty depend on the messy competition between society and elites (and state 906 Perspectives on Politics Critical Dialogue https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592720001863

institutions), where each side has to run as fast as it can just to keep up with the other. Berman also provides a very plausible connection between this history and the current malaise of liberal democracy. Yet, like all good works of social science, the book raises many questions to investigate further and debate. Let us focus on two here. The ﬁrst is the issue of sequencing, which is critical to Berman’s conceptual framework. Is it right, as Berman claims, that liberal democracy emerges from a particular sequence: state-national identity ﬁrst and liberal democracy following later? We are not sure. There are two parts to this claim, one relating to identity that we will discuss in the context of our next point and another related to the view that state development must precede liberal democracy; for example, as claimed by Francis Fukuyama in his inﬂuential book, The Origins of Political Order: From Prehuman Times to the French Revolution (2011). Much evidence goes against this sequencing. As we argue in our book, the typical pattern is one in which state capacity develops at the same time as democratic political participation. There are certainly many examples of nondemocratic, despotic strong states in history, but they often use their unaccountable power to block democracy, rather than preparing the ground for it. More tellingly, in most cases despotic states do not develop the deepest form of state capacity, because they lack both cooperation from society and the impetus that comes from society’s powerful challenges. Put diﬀerently, without the Red Queen eﬀect, state capacity remains ultimately limited. The British case, in fact, far from supporting the sequencing at the center of Berman’s conceptualization, vividly illustrates the simul- taneous development of state institutions and a more mobilized and democratically empowered society (Charles Tilly, Popular Contention in Great Britain, 1998, being perhaps the best empirical articulation of this pattern). Berman’s conceptual account also places great emphasis on favorable initial conditions, emphasizing again the British case as an exemplar. But where do these favorable conditions come from? The book takes its cue from the perspective oﬀered by Eugene Weber (1976) in his seminal book Peasants into Frenchmen: The Modernization of Rural France, 1870–1914. In this account, the path to modernity goes through the development of a powerful state that then socializes its citizens. Yet, it is clear that Britain took no such path. Arguably, there was a notion of being English already at the time that the Venerable Bede wrote in the seventh century—long before there was any powerful English or British state. Indeed, the state had no tools for eﬀective socialization until the Elementary Education Act of 1870. England made a pathetic hash in the eighteenth century of trying to socialize the Scots into being British by banning the wearing of kilts. Yet this policy was worse than ineﬀec- tual; it seems to have led to a backlash and made Scots even more Scottish (see Hugh Trevor-Roper, “The Invention of Tradition: The Highland Tradition of Scotland,” in Eric Hobsbawm and Terence O. Ranger, eds., The Invention of Tradition, 1983). The fact that state socialization may have such eﬀects seems even to be true in the United States, an apparent poster child for the creation of a national identity. Eﬀorts to erase German identity in the United States appear to have increased parents’ willingness to invest in the German identity of their children (Vasiliki Fouka, “Back- lash: The Unintended Eﬀects of Language Prohibition in U.S. Schools after World War I,” Review of Economic Studies 87 [1], 2020). Not only was there never a British identity but the English identity also does not seem to have been created by the state. Benedict Anderson (Imagined Communities: Reﬂections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism, 1983) argued that it was the decay of hierarchical notions of society and the emergence of “print capitalism” that created national identity. The state features almost nowhere in his argument, except as an employer of people who could buy books and newspapers. Locke himself, in an essay in 1693, observed that what really deﬁned English identity was assenting to and obeying the common law, which was at least a partially bottom-up project. Many attempts to characterize the core of English identity similarly turn to features unrelated to the state as its deﬁning features. George Orwell (The Lion and the Unicorn, 1941), for example, follows Locke in his emphasis on the law and also notes the “privateness of English life”: he argues, “All the culture that is most truly native centres round things which even when they are communal are not oﬃcial—the pub, the football match, the back garden, the ﬁreside and the ‘nice cup of tea.’” In other words, what is critical for Englishness is not anything deﬁned by the state, but rather the autonomous spaces outside the reach of the state. Itiseasytothinkofotherexamples,liketheFinnsor Kurds, who have historically developed very powerful “national” identities with no states and thereafter went in search of a state. This all suggests that national identity is not the universal precondition and that, when it develops, it often does so without an active guiding hand from a state-building project. None of this is to say Berman is wrong in her emphasis on the importance of identity, arguably even national identity (even if Britain seems not to have had it). Our point is that the roots of these identities are much more varied in interesting and important ways. Response to Daron Acemoglu and James A. Democracy and Dictatorship September 2020 | Vol. 18/No. 3 907 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592720001863

argues that consolidated liberal democracy requires a fairly strong state and sense of national identity, but it does not argue that “liberal democracy emerges from a particular sequence,” as they put it, with “state-national identity ﬁrst and liberal democracy following later.” In fact, Democracy and Dictatorship argues that there were many sequences of state, nation, and democracy development in Europe— none of which were simple, straightforward, or easy. In Western Europe, the pattern that Acemoglu and Robinson emphasize occurred—state-building, followed by nation-building and then stable democracy—but Dem- ocracy and Dictatorship stresses that even countries in this region took a long time to achieve stable democracy and had to endure conﬂict, violence, and backsliding along the way. France began modern state-building under the ancien régime. But this state-building stalled, contributing to the outbreak of the French Revolution. The revolution then began the modern struggle for democracy and propelled French state and nation-building forward. But despite the early start of state- and nation-building in France, it took another century and a half of struggle after 1789 to achieve stable democracy with the Fifth Republic. Even Britain, the clearest case of the state- and nation-building before dem- ocracy sequence, and the case often held up as the paradigm of peaceful political development, required the tumult of the seventeenth-century civil wars and Glorious Revolution to put it on this path. After 1688 state-building was propelled forward, as was the often-forcible uniﬁcation of the parts of the British Isles, but it took centuries more until universal manhood suﬀrage was achieved in 1918. In Central, Southern, and Eastern Europe, the sequen- cing of state, nation, and democracy development diﬀered. But the diﬀerence between these regions and Western Europe concerned not whether liberal democracy could be achieved or how much violence and instability were part of its backstory, but rather when and over how long a period this violence and instability occurred. In Spain state- and nation-building began in the early modern period but then stalled, and so the challenge of democratization had to be faced with a weak state and national identity—contributing to the high levels of political instability and violence the country experi- enced during the nineteenth and much of the twentieth centuries, before achieving stable democracy at the end of the twentieth. In Italy, a national state emerged in the late nineteenth century and then soon thereafter con- fronted the challenges of nation-building and democra- tization. Italy quickly collapsed into political disorder and violence, culminating in fascism, before achieving a fairly stable democracy after 1945. In Eastern Europe, independent countries only emerged at the end of World War I and, as in other newly decolonized regions, had to confront the challenges of building a state, nation, and democracy simultaneously. This proved overwhelming, and these countries’ initial democratic experiments quickly failed. After several more decades of colonization, East European countries transitioned again to democracy in 1989, but these democratic experiments have proven fragile. Given the history of democratic development in Western, Central, and Southern Europe, this should not surprise us, because none of these regions experienced rapid, linear demo- cratic development. Again, a key lesson of Democracy and Dictatorship is how diﬃcult achieving successful liberal democracy is, precisely because it requires myriad political, social, and economic conditions to be in place. Among the most important of these are indeed a strong state, along the lines traced out by Acemoglu and Robinson in The Narrow Corridor, as well as a fairly strong sense of national identity and unity. But there was no “particular sequence” that enabled them to develop simply or easily.
